description: Somos Intinova, un equipo de Ingeniería en Cajamarca, Perú, apasionados por la tecnología, la ciencia y la innovación. Combinamos nuestras habilidades en desarrollo de software, análisis de datos y trabajo colaborativo para crear soluciones tecnológicas que respondan a desafíos reales y generen un impacto positivo en nuestro planeta.
summary:
IntiFire is a web app that turns NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one harmonized fire calendar for Peru, from November 2000 to today.

MODIS and VIIRS see fire differently, so their counts cannot be added. We scale MODIS to the VIIRS scale with one factor per month; on 60 unseen months the median error for the whole country was 9.6%. After that the sensor no longer matters, only patterns, trends and anomalies.

Analysts pick the country, a department, province, protected area or their own area, choose dates, compare the current month with the historical median, and download the series, the hotspots (CSV) and the calendar.

For everyone, the same data is playable: the public view answers "is there fire near me, and is it normal?", and Culli, our guide (a real Peruvian hummingbird threatened by fire), leads a time machine, a quiz and a puzzle of Peru.

For responders, an operations view shows active events and a fire-spread simulation, and an experimental model estimates 72-hour fire risk in Cajamarca from hotspot history, weather and vegetation.

Why it matters: as MODIS ages and VIIRS takes over, 25 years of fire history stay comparable. Knowing what is normal lets families, analysts and responders notice when a fire is not.
details:
What it does. IntiFire is a web platform that harmonizes NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) into one continuous fire-activity series for Peru, from November 2000 to today. Because the two sensors differ in sensitivity (the VIIRS/MODIS ratio ranges from about 3.4 to 7.5 and varies by month), we convert MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale using monthly factors calibrated on the overlap period, and fill the most recent days with VIIRS NOAA-20. A hold-out test (factors fitted before 2020, tested on the 60 months from 2020) gave a median absolute error of 9.6% for the whole country. Estimated and preliminary stretches are clearly marked.

How it works. Users explore a unified calendar (by month, by day and anomalies) for the country, any department, province, protected area or custom area (a drawn polygon or a point with a radius), pick a range of years, and compare current activity with the historical median for that time of year, including El Niño and La Niña years. There are three views: a public view (is there fire near me, and is it normal?), a professional panel (when and where does this territory burn?), and an operations view (where to send people first), with community fire reports, a one-click fire-spread simulation and an experimental 72-hour risk forecast for Cajamarca (XGBoost model, 10 km cells, calibrated probabilities).

Benefits and impact. It turns two incompatible satellite records into a single 25-year baseline that anyone can read, helping communities, researchers, park authorities and emergency teams spot abnormal fire seasons early and prioritize response. Data can be downloaded (CSV, GeoJSON, PNG). It works on desktop, tablet and phone, in light and dark themes, in English and Spanish, with a guided tour in every view.

Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, ECharts, Three.js and Tailwind CSS (frontend); Python, FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn and XGBoost (backend); deployed on Railway with Docker. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS), NASA GIBS, MODIS NDVI, NOAA ONI, geoBoundaries, SERNANP protected areas, ERA5-Land and Open-Meteo weather. No special hardware is needed: it runs in any modern browser, including phones.

Creativity. The same data is playable. Culli, our mascot, is a grey-bellied comet, a hummingbird endemic to northern Peru and threatened by burning, who guides users through a landing page with the satellites in 3D, a time machine across 25 years, a quiz answered before seeing the real figures and a puzzle of Peru's departments. We pair scientific rigor with accessibility for non-experts.

Factors considered. Transparency (a hotspot is a satellite detection, not a confirmed fire), honest uncertainty (validation error shown, estimated and experimental parts labeled), privacy and abuse protection for community reports (rate limits, duplicate detection, hashed visitor IDs, moderation), and API-key protection for FIRMS. Known limits: it covers Peru only; the harmonization was validated at country level and has not yet been reviewed by a fire scientist; the risk forecast is experimental and limited to Cajamarca.

Use of AI. Much of the code and documentation was written with AI coding assistants (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex), directed and reviewed by the team. Culli is an AI-generated image and carries a visible "AI-generated image" label. The demo video's voice-over was generated with text-to-speech; its picture is a screen recording of the live app. The data is not generated: it comes from the sources listed below.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS - MODIS and VIIRS active fire data (country archive)
NASA GIBS - Blue Marble Shaded Relief and Bathymetry imagery
NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 - 16-day NDVI (vegetation input of the risk model)
NASA Space Apps Challenge - Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
projectRefs: NOAA Climate Prediction Center - Oceanic Nino Index (El Nino and La Nina years)
Open-Meteo - weather forecast and wind (fire simulation and risk forecast)
Copernicus ERA5-Land - climate data used to train the risk model
Terrain Tiles (Terrarium, AWS Open Data) - relief and elevation
CARTO basemaps - Dark Matter map style
Cuadros and Angulo (2023), Bird Conservation International 33, e51 - Grey-bellied Comet data (Culli)
MapLibre GL JS - interactive maps (open source)
scikit-learn - model calibration and evaluation (open source)
